'''''Centaurea solstitialis''''', the '''yellow star-thistle''', is a species of thorny plant in the genus ''[[Centaurea]]'', which is part of the family [[Asteraceae]]. A [[winter annual]], it is native to the [[Mediterranean Basin]] region and [[Invasive species|invasive]] in many other places. It is also known as '''golden starthistle''', '''yellow cockspur''' and '''St. Barnaby's thistle''' (or '''Barnaby thistle''').<ref>{{cite web|last=DiTomaso |first=J |title=Element Stewarship Abstract for ''Centaurea solstitialis'' |publisher=[[The Nature Conservancy]] |year=2001 |url=http://tncweeds.ucdavis.edu/esadocs/documnts/centsol.pdf |accessdate=2007-06-01 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070221130956/http://tncweeds.ucdavis.edu/esadocs/documnts/centsol.pdf |archivedate=2007-02-21 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Description==
''Centaurea solstitialis'' is an [[Annual plant|annual]] herb from the family [[Asteraceae]]. During the vegetative stage it forms a [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]] of non-spiny [[leaves]], between {{Convert|5–20|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} in diameter. As the summer approaches, it produces a flowering stem up to {{Convert|1|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} in height.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/364/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |pages=364 |orig-date=1979}}</ref> The leaves at the base are lobed and range between {{Convert|5–8|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} in length, while the ones on the stem are unlobed and smaller.<ref name=":0" /> Between May and October, the stem produces numerous spinous [[flower heads]] (capitula) about {{Convert|12-16|mm|frac=8}} across, containing between 10 and 50 yellow flowers, with [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|spines]] between {{Convert|1-2.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}}.<ref name=":0" /> Flowers within capitula are [[pollinated]] by [[insects]] and each capitula produces 10–50 seeds, some with and some without a [[Pappus (botany)|pappus]]. It is an annual [[semelparous]] species, and will die after reproduction is completed, normally by the end of the summer.

=== Similar species ===
Similar species include purple star-thistle (''[[Centaurea calcitrapa]]''), sulphur star-thistle (''[[Centaurea sulphurea|C. sulphurea]]''), Maltese star-thistle (''[[Centaurea melitensis|C. melitensis]]''), and rough star-thistle (''[[Centaurea aspera|C. aspera]]'').<ref name="The Wild Flower Key">{{cite book |last=Rose |first=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |publisher=Frederick Warne & Co |year=1981 |isbn=0-7232-2419-6 |pages=386–387 |authorlink=Francis Rose}}</ref> Bachelor's button (''[[Centaurea cyanus|C. cyaneus]]'') is a relative.<ref name=":0" />

==Ecology==
''Centaurea solstitialis'' is considered a [[weed]] also on its [[Native species|native]] European range (e.g., [[Turkey]], [[Greece]], [[Italy]], [[France]], [[Spain]]). Consequently, it inhabits highly disturbed [[ruderal]] [[habitats]], being typically found on roadsides and cereal crop margins. After introduction in several parts of the world as an [[exotic species]] (e.g., [[Australia]], [[Argentina]], [[Chile]], the [[United States]]),<ref name="gbif.org">{{Cite web | url=https://www.gbif.org |title = GBIF}}</ref> it has developed local adaptations to the different habitats colonized,<ref>Hierro, J. L., Eren, Ö., Khetsuriani, L., Diaconu, A., Török, K., Montesinos, D., … Callaway, R. M. (2009). Germination responses of an invasive species in native and non-native ranges. Oikos, 118(4), 529–538. doi:10.1111/j.1600-0706.2009.17283.x</ref><ref>Graebner, R. C., Callaway, R. M., & Montesinos, D. (2012). Invasive species grows faster, competes better, and shows greater evolution toward increased seed size and growth than exotic non-invasive congeners. Plant Ecology, 213(4), 545–553. doi:10.1007/s11258-012-0020-x</ref> and an incipient level of reproductive isolation between native and non-native ranges has been detected<ref>Montesinos, D., Santiago, G., & Callaway, R. M. (2012). Neo-allopatry and rapid reproductive isolation. The American Naturalist, 180(4), 529–33. doi:10.1086/667585</ref>—a case of [[ecological speciation]].

Star-thistle is a valuable source of pollen, thus [[nectar]] for pollinators. Yellow star-thistle, a noted pest plant in California, is a major nectar source for many butterflies of the state's central valleys and foothills.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Toby Hemenway - Author & Permaculturalist |url=http://www.patternliteracy.com/644-saving-native-wildlife-with-invasive-plants}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=YELLOW STAR-THISTLE |url=https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/plantmaterials/mtpmspg10613.pdf}} [[Natural Resources Conservation Service|USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service]]. Retrieved on 2026-02-02.</ref> Star-thistle populates ground that has been abused: dry, compacted, or scraped clean. A plant with a [[taproot]] system, it has a crucial role in restoring the soil by bringing up vital micronutrients. Similar to many plants classified as 'weeds', they (in the words of Mark Schonbeck) "quickly establish in, protect, and restore soil that has been left exposed by natural and human-caused disturbances".<ref>{{Cite web |title=An Ecological Understanding of Weeds - eXtension |url=http://www.extension.org/pages/18529/an-ecological-understanding-of-weeds#.VXnl8M7BLGk |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151005152755/http://www.extension.org/pages/18529/an-ecological-understanding-of-weeds#.VXnl8M7BLGk |archive-date=2015-10-05 |access-date=2015-06-11}}</ref>

''C. solstitialis'' grows as a balanced part of the [[ecosystems]] in [[Eurasia]], where it is kept in check by an assortment of natural [[herbivore]] enemies and other plants that have {{Nowrap|[[Coevolution|co-evolved]]}} with it in its native habitat. However, it has been introduced in several parts of the world, including Australia, Argentina, Chile, and the U.S.<ref name="gbif.org" /> In many of these non-native regions, where the particular array of natural biological controls found in the native regions do not exist, it has become an [[invasive species]] and [[noxious weed]].

The yellow star-thistle plant has the ability to create [[monotypic]] stands and habitats in the cultivated soil of fields, graded dirt sites, and disturbed natural ecosystem lands. Its [[colonization]] eliminates and prevents other plant species from growing, terminating the habitat's [[biodiversity]]. Extensive spreading monotypic fields of yellow star-thistle are not uncommon. Its growth plasticity, competitiveness, preference for the Mediterranean climate, and a lack of natural herbivore enemies and co-evolved species, make it a very successful invader. The plant is an invasive pest in field crops, degrades native plant habitats and natural ecosystems, prevents the grazing of [[domestic animals]] in [[rangeland]]s, and is a physical barrier to indigenous animal movement in wildlands.<ref>[https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/profile/yellow-star-thistle Yellow star-thistle species profile] from the [[United States Department of Agriculture|U.S. Department of Agriculture]] National Invasive Species Information Center</ref>

=== As an invasive species ===
The introduction of ''C. solstitialis'' in [[North America]] probably occurred in [[California]] sometime after the start of the [[California Gold Rush]], as a [[fodder]] seed contaminant in imported [[Agriculture in Chile|Chilean-harvested]] [[alfalfa]] seed, also known as Chilean clover (''[[Trifolium macraei]]'').<ref name="ucd">[http://wric.ucdavis.edu/yst/ Yellow Starthistle Information] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050711074228/http://wric.ucdavis.edu/yst/|date=2005-07-11}} from a [[University of California, Davis]] (UCD) website</ref> Star-thistle has been introduced throughout North and South America, Africa, and Europe.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Directorate |first=Government of Canada, Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Plant Health and Biosecurity |date=2012-03-15 |title=Yellow starthistle – Centaurea solstitialis L. |url=https://www.inspection.gc.ca/plants/plant-pests-invasive-species/invasive-plants/fact-sheets/yellow-starthistle/eng/1331825936442/1331826040057 |access-date=2016-03-01 |website=www.inspection.gc.ca}}</ref>

In California, yellow star-thistle was dispersed into agricultural fields and immediately took hold in the state's areas with a [[Mediterranean climate]]. [[Human factors]], such as mowing, land grading for development and roads, domestic animal grazing, and disturbance of the soil surface for agricultural [[tillage]] and wildland [[firebreak]]s have and continue to contribute to the successful thriving and spread of this plant. Yellow star-thistle is now a very common sight in vacant lots and fields, along roadsides and trails, in pastures and ranch lands, and in parks, open-space preserves and natural areas.

After the turn of the 20th century, Spain, France, Italy, and perhaps [[Turkestan]] were also likely sources of the invasion's seed in California.<ref name="ucd" /> Since its introduction to California in the mid-19th century,<ref name="ucd" /> it has become a large-scale invasive species (noxious weed or invasive exotic) throughout 23 [[U.S. state]]s. It currently dominates over {{convert|15000000|acre|km2|abbr=off}} in California alone.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mount Diablo Review, Autumn 2007 |url=http://www.mdia.org/PDF%20Files/MD%20Review%20Autumn2007.pdf}}{{dead link|date=August 2017|bot=InternetArchiveBot|fix-attempted=yes}} {{small|(286 [[Kibibyte|KiB]])}}, [[Mount Diablo]] Interpretive Association. Retrieved on 2008-10-15.</ref><ref name="wric.ucdavis.edu">[http://wric.ucdavis.edu/yst/images/none/nc4.JPG 1970 UCD Yellow Starthistle Information website - Map of Distribution of yellow star-thistle in the U.S.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061231024708/http://wric.ucdavis.edu/yst/images/none/nc4.JPG|date=December 31, 2006}}</ref>

By 1970,<ref name="wric.ucdavis.edu" /> yellow star-thistle had reached 23 U.S. states.<ref name="ucd" />  According to the [[U.S. Forest Service]], as of 2006 the plant has been reported present in 41 of the 48 [[contiguous U.S.]] states, with the only exceptions being [[Maine]], [[Vermont]], and five of the [[Deep South]] states ([[Arkansas]], [[Louisiana]], [[Mississippi]], [[Alabama]], and [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]).<ref name="USFS">{{cite web |title=Yellow Star-thistle species profile |url=http://www.na.fs.fed.us/fhp/invasive_plants/weeds/yellow-starthistle.pdf}} {{small|(179 [[Kibibyte|KiB]])}}, [[United States Forest Service|USDA Forest Service]]. Retrieved on 2008-10-15.</ref> The plant is considered an invasive species in six of the 41 states: California, [[Oregon]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]], [[Idaho]], [[Utah]], and [[New Jersey]].

[[File: Centaurea solstitialis 2.jpg|thumb|''C. solstitialis'' in [[Klickitat County, Washington]]]]

==== Chemical control ====
Most herbicides used for controlling yellow star-thistle are registered for range lands, right-of-way, and other non-crop areas. Many [[auxin]]-like or growth-regulator herbicides are used for post-emergence control, including {{Nowrap|[[2,4-D]]}}, [[aminopyralid]], [[clopyralid]], [[dicamba]], [[picloram]] and [[triclopyr]]. In California, [[aminopyralid]], which has both post- and preemergence activity,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=DiTomaso |first1=Joseph |title=Linking Ecological Principles to Tools and Strategies in an EBIPM Program |journal=Rangelands |date=December 2012 |volume=34 |issue=6 |pages=30–34 |doi=10.2111/RANGELANDS-D-12-00060.1 |url=https://doi.org/10.2111/RANGELANDS-D-12-00060.1|hdl=10150/639926 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> is the most commonly used,<ref name="DiTomaso 2012">{{cite journal |last1=DiTomaso |first1=Joseph |title=Effects of Aminopyralid on California Annual Grassland Plant Communities |journal=Invasive Plant Science and Management |date=January–March 2015 |volume=8 |pages=98–109 |doi=10.1614/IPSM-D-14-00010.1}}</ref> most effectively after an early summer prescribed burn.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=DiTomaso |first1=Joseph |title=Control of Invasive Weeds with Prescribed Burning |journal=Weed Technology |date=2006 |volume=20 |pages=535–548}}</ref> Alternatively, [[glyphosate]] may be used. Pre-emergence herbicides used for yellow star-thistle control include chlorsulfuron and sulfometuron. Pre-emergence and post-emergence herbicides may be used effectively together to kill growing plants as well as any new seedlings that may emerge from the copious [[soil seed bank]] often produced by yellow star-thistle. Controlled burning may also be used in conjunction with clopyralid application as an effective integrated approach to yellow star-thistle management.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ipm.ucdavis.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7402.html |title=UC IPM Online |publisher=Ipm.ucdavis.edu |date=2005-05-20 |accessdate=2012-04-28}}</ref>

[[Aminocyclopyrachlor]] + [[chlorsulfuron]], [[aminopyralid]], chlorsulfuron, [[clopyralid]], clopyralid + 2,4-D, dicamba, [[diflufenzopyr]] + dicamba, picloram, and [[triclopyr]] + clopyralid for the [[Pacific Northwest]] of North America.<ref name="PNWHB" />

A yellow star-thistle biotype [[herbicide resistance|resistant]] to picloram was discovered in a pasture near [[Dayton, Ohio]], in 1988. This biotype was determined to have [[cross-resistance|cross resistance]] to other auxin-like herbicides, especially clopyralid.<ref>Fuerst E.P., Sterling T.M., Norman M.A., Prather T.S., Irzyk G.P., Wu Y., Lownds N.K., and Callihan R.H., 1996. Physiological characterization of picloram resistance in yellow star-thistle. Pest Biochem Physiol 56:149–161.</ref> Resistance was discovered to be conveyed by a single nuclear recessive gene.<ref>Sabba R.P., Ray I.M., Lownds N. and Sterling T.N., 2003. Inheritance of resistance to clopyralid and picloram in yellow star-thistle (''Centaurea solstitialis'' L.) is controlled by a single nuclear recessive gene. J. Heredity 94(6): 523-527.</ref>

Picloram-resistant ''C. solstitialis'' has been observed which had cross-resistance to clopyralid, dicamba, and [[fluroxypyr]], but not triclopyr or 2,4-D.<ref name="Alberta" />

==== Biological control ====
[[File:Yellow Star Thistle.jpg|thumb|Specimen in California in autumn]]

Yellow star-thistle is sometimes resistant to removal methods such as mowing and burning, because of its long root system and the seeds' ability to withstand fire. The plant has been the target of [[biological pest control]] programs with positive results. Seven types of seed-feeding insects have been released (one accidentally) to control the plant.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.invasive.org/weedcd/pdfs/StarthistleBook.pdf |title=Biology and Biological Control of Yellow Starthistle |date= |accessdate=2012-04-28}}</ref><ref>Pitcairn, M. J., B.Villegas, D. M. Woods, R. Yacoub, and D. B. Joley. 2008. Evaluating implementation success for seven seed head insects on Centaurea solstitialis in California, USA, pp. 610-616. In M. H. Julien, R. Sforza, M. C. Bon, H. C. Evans, P. E. Hatcher, H. L. Hinz, and B. G. Rector (eds.), Proceedings of the XII International Symposium on Biological Control of Weeds. La Grande Motte, Montpellier, France (in press).</ref>

===== Insects =====
Three species of [[weevil]] in the beetle subfamily Cleoninae effectively reduce seed production in the yellow star-thistle.
* Yellow star-thistle bud weevil (''[[Bangasternus orientalis]]'') is a fuzzy brown weevil that lays its eggs in the flowers, and when its larvae hatch, they feed on the developing seed.<ref>Campobasso, G.; Sobhian, R.; Knutson, L.; Terragitti, G. 1998. Host specificity of Bangasternus orientalis Capiomont (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) introduced into the United States for biological control of yellow starthistle (Centaurea solstitialis L., Asteraceae: Carduae). Environmental entomology,. v. 27 (6), pp. 1525–1530.</ref>
* Yellow star-thistle hairy weevil (''[[Eustenopus villosus]]'') is a long-snouted, hairy-looking weevil that lays a single egg inside each flower bud. The larva then consumes the seeds within.<ref>Fornasari, L., and R. Sobhain. 1993. Life history of ''Eustenopus villosus'' (Coleoptera' Curculionidae), a promising biological control agent for yellow starthistle. Environ. Entomol. 22: 684-692.</ref><ref>Connett, J.F.; Wilson, L.M.; McCaffrey, J.P.; Harmon, B.L. 2001. Phenological synchrony of ''Eustenopus villosus'' (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) with Centaurea solstitialis in Idaho. Environmental entomology, v. 30 (2), pp. 439–442.</ref>
* Yellow star-thistle flower weevil (''[[Larinus curtus]]'') is a brownish weevil that lays eggs in the flowers as it feeds on the pollen. The larvae then eat the seeds when they hatch.<ref>Fornasari, L. and C.E. Turner. 1992. Host specificity of the Palearctic weevil ''Larinus curtus'' Hochut (Coleoptera: Curculionidae), a natural enemy of ''Centaurea solstitialis'' L. (Asteraceae: Cardueae). In: Proceedings of the Eighth International Symposium on Biological Control of Weeds. 2–7 February 1992. Lincoln University, Canter- 1bury, New Zealand, 385-391</ref> This insect has failed to established dense populations in the United States.<ref>Pitcairn, M. J., G. L. Piper, and E. M. Coombs. 2004. Yellow starthistle, pp. 421-435. In E. M. Coombs, J. K. Clark, G. L. Piper, and A. F. Cofrancesco, Jr. (eds.), Biological control of invasive plants in the United States. Oregon State University Press, Corvallis, OR</ref><ref>Pitcairn, M. J., D. M. Woods, and V. Popescu. 2005. Update on the long-term monitoring of the combined impact of biological control insects on yellow starthistle, pp. 27-30. In D. M. Woods (ed.), Biological control program annual summary, 2004. California Department of Food and Agriculture, Plant Health and Pest Prevention Services, Sacramento, CA</ref>
Four species of [[Tephritidae|tephritid fruit fly]] also attack the [[Head (botany)|seedhead]]s of yellow star-thistle.
* Yellow star-thistle peacock fly and false peacock fly (''[[Chaetorellia australis]]'' and ''[[Chaetorellia succinea]]'', respectively, the latter released unintentionally) are small nectar-feeding flies that deposit eggs into the seedheads, where their larvae consume the seeds and flower ovaries.<ref>Turner, C.E., G.L. Piper and E.M. Coombs. 1996. ''Chaetorellia australis'' (Diptera: Tephritidae) for biological control of yellow starthistle, ''Centaurea solstitialis'' (Compositae), in the western USA: establishment and seed destruction. Bull. Entomol. Res. 86: 1 77-182.</ref>
* Banded yellow star-thistle gall fly (''[[Urophora sirunaseva]]'') produces larvae that pupate within a woody [[gall]] within the flower and disrupt seed production.<ref>Sobhian, R. 1993. Life history and host specificity of ''Urophora sirunaseva''
(Herng)(Dipt., Tephritidae), an agent for biological control of yellow starthistle, with remarks on the host plant. J. Appl. Entomol. 116: 381–390.</ref>
* Another gall fly ''Urophora jaculata'' was released in 1969 but never established.<ref>Turner, C.E., Johnson, J.B., McCaffrey, J.P., 1994. Yellow starthistle, ''Centaurea solstitialis'' L. (Asteraceae). In: Nechols, J.R. (Ed.),
Biological Control in the U.S. Western Region: Accomplishments and Benefits of Regional Research Project W-84 (1964-1989). Division of Agriculture and Natural Research, University of California, Berkeley, pp. 274–279</ref>

===== Fungi =====
A variety of the [[rust fungus]] [[Puccinia jaceae var. solstitialis|''Puccinia jaceae'' var. ''solstitialis'']], first released in July 2003 on a ranch in the [[Napa Valley]], has shown promise as an agent against yellow star-thistle,<ref>[https://agresearchmag.ars.usda.gov/2004/aug/fungus Fungus Unleashed To Combat Yellow Star-thistle] from the [[United States Department of Agriculture|U.S. Department of Agriculture]] website</ref><ref name="OBrien-et-al-2010" /> dramatically damaging leaves and hampering growth.<ref name="OBrien-et-al-2010" /> The rust causes widespread pathology in the leaves of the plant and slows its dispersal. The fungus ''Synchytrium solstitiale'' (''[[Synchytrium]]'' of phylum [[Chytridiomycota]]) is also being considered as an agent of biological control.<ref name="Gleason">Voigt K., A.V. Marano, & F.H. Gleason. 2013. Ecological & Economical Importance of Parasitic Zoosporic True Fungi. ''in'': The Mycota: A Comprehensive Treatise on Fungi as Experimental Systems for Basic & Applied Research Vol. 11 Agricultural Applications. 2nd edition Eds: K. Esser & F. Kempken. New York: Springer pp. 243–270.</ref>

===== Grazing =====
Grazing by goats, cattle, or sheep can be effective in controlling yellow star-thistle.<ref>[http://wric.ucdavis.edu/yst/manage/management3.html] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100611164008/http://wric.ucdavis.edu/yst/manage/management3.html |date=June 11, 2010 }}</ref> Goats will eat star-thistle even in its spiny stage.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ipm.ucdavis.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7402.html |title=Yellow Starthistle Management Guidelines-UC IPM |publisher=Ipm.ucdavis.edu |date=2005-05-20 |accessdate=2012-04-28}}</ref> Because yellow star-thistle growth is particularly difficult to inhibit in canyon rangelands since its remoteness limits control options, goats and other herbivores have become an excellent option to curb the plant's spread. According to one study, grazing has decreased yellow star-thistle presence by 58% when compared to the study's [[Scientific control|controls]]. Subplots also showed a 94% decrease in seed heads after only three years of experimentation.<ref>{{Cite journal| last1 = Goehring| first1 = Brianna J.| last2 = Launchbaugh| first2 = Karen L.| last3 = Wilson| first3 = Linda M.| date = 2010-04-01| title = Late-Season Targeted Grazing of Yellow Starthistle (''Centaurea solstitialis'') with Goats in Idaho| journal = Invasive Plant Science and Management| volume = 3| issue = 2| pages = 148–154| doi = 10.1614/IPSM-D-09-00004.1| s2cid = 86184511| issn = 1939-7291}}</ref>

===== Integrated methods =====
California researchers (Thomsen et al., 1996) tested mowing, controlled sheep grazing and subterranean clover plantings to control star-thistle growth. According to the researchers, subclover would help fill the void left by star-thistle populations.<ref>{{Cite web |url= http://www.agrisk.umn.edu/cache/ARL02967.htm |title= Thistle Control Alternatives |website= www.agrisk.umn.edu |access-date= 2016-03-01 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160314110021/http://www.agrisk.umn.edu/cache/ARL02967.htm |archive-date = 2016-03-14 |url-status= dead}}</ref>

They compared subclover seeding, grazing, two mowings, grazing + mowing without subclover – and an untouched control without grazing, subclover, or mowing. Thistle seed production was 130 times higher where only one mowing was done, and 1,720 times higher where nothing was done, as compared to the area that had been grazed and mowed twice. Excellent yellow star-thistle control can be achieved with the combination of competing plants, mowing, and [[rotational grazing]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.groworganic.com/organic-gardening/articles/natural-control-of-yellow-star-thistle |title=Natural Control of Yellow Star Thistle | Organic Gardening Blog |access-date=2015-06-11 |archive-date=2016-06-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160608011936/http://www.groworganic.com/organic-gardening/articles/natural-control-of-yellow-star-thistle |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===== Research =====
Although these [[biocontrol]] agents have proven somewhat effective at controlling ''Centaurea solstitialis'', there is interest in finding additional agents to further control the species. Two weevils, including ''[[Larinus filiformis]]'', a flowerhead feeding weevil, and ''Ceratapion basicorne'' (Illiger) (Coleoptera: Apionidae), which develops in the root crown of rosettes have been evaluated and proposed for introduction.<ref>Smith, L. 2007. Physiological host range of ''Ceratapion basicorne'', a prospective biological control agent of ''Centaurea solstitialis'' (Asteraceae). Biol. Control 41: 120-133.</ref> Also under evaluation are a stem-feeding flea beetle ''Psylliodes chalcomera'' (Illiger) (Coleoptera: Chrysomelidae) (Cristofaro et al. 2004a), a lacebug ''Tingis grisea'' Germar (Heteroptera: Tingidae), and a mite ''Aceria solstitialis'' de Lillo (Acari: Eriophyidae).<ref>de Lillo et al. 2003</ref><ref>Smith, L. 2004. Prospective new agents for biological control of yellow starthistle, pp. 136-138. Proceedings 56th Annual California Weed Science Society, 12–14 January 2004, Sacramento, CA</ref>

== Toxicity ==
Grazing of the plant by horses can cause [[nigropallidal encephalomalacia]] or "chewing disease", a neurological condition. The disease generally follows consumption of 60–200% of the horse's body weight over an extended period of a month or more, or {{Convert|2.3–2.6|kg|abbr=off}} of star-thistle per {{Convert|100|kg|abbr=on}} body weight per day. Though star-thistle is most dangerous when it is the only plant available or is delivered as a contaminant in dried hay, horses may develop a taste for it and seek it out. Many other grazing species, including mules and burros, are not affected.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Joseph M. Ditomaso |author2=Guy B. Kyser |author3=Michael J. Pitcairn |date=June 2006 |title=Yellow Starthistle Management Guide |url=http://www.cal-ipc.org/ip/management/pdf/YSTMgmtweb.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160917175539/http://www.cal-ipc.org/ip/management/pdf/YSTMgmtweb.pdf |archive-date=2016-09-17 |access-date=2016-09-06 |publisher=California Invasive Plant Council}}</ref>

== Uses ==
Although the spines make the plant a pain to deal with, it produces a light honey.<ref name=":0" />
